html:
Siddhartha Gautama, called the Buddha, "the awakened one", was a wandering teacher of the eastern Ganges plain who founded Buddhism. Tradition dates his life to 563 to 483 BCE, but many scholars now place it later, with his death around 400 BCE.

By Buddhist tradition he was born at Lumbini, now in Nepal, son of a chief of the Shakya clan. Two centuries later Ashoka marked the spot with a pillar. At about 29 he left his wife, child and comfortable life to become a wandering ascetic. Years of fasting brought no answer, so he chose a "middle way" between pleasure and self-torment. Meditating under a tree at Bodh Gaya he reached awakening.

He spent some 45 years teaching in the kingdoms of the Mahajanapadas, above all Magadha and Kosala, and founded an order of monks and later of nuns. His teaching is described under The Buddha teaches. He died at about 80 at Kushinagar, and his ashes were divided among several peoples and enshrined in stupas.

He was one of several teachers of his time who broke with Vedic ritual; Mahavira, founder of Jainism as we know it, was a contemporary. His words were passed on by memory and first written down in the Pali Canon in Sri Lanka in the 1st century BCE.

From India his teaching spread to Sri Lanka, Central Asia, China, Korea, Japan, Tibet and Southeast Asia. Today hundreds of millions follow it.
